newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egypt militants call for unilateral truce.
newsitem.headline: Egypt militants call for unilateral truce.

text.p: Five imprisoned leaders of the main Moslem militant group in Egypt have asked their followers to stop unilaterally all acts of violence, a lawyer close to the Islamist movement said on Sunday.

Amin Abdul Alim, one of the defendants in the trial of 97 alleged Islamist militants, read out a ceasefire appeal from the Gama'a al-Islamiya (Islamic Group) leaders in court on Saturday but it was not clear what authority he had to speak for them.
On Sunday one of the defence lawyers, Muntasser el-Zayyat, said: "I confirm the statement is genuine, because Abdul Alim gave me signs...that he was speaking on behalf of the five."

"I am optimistic that it will be observed, because those five have spiritual weight -- they are the founding leadership of the Gama'a," added the lawyer, an Islamist known for his close contacts with the militants.
The Gama'a has been fighting the security forces since 1992 in a low-level guerrilla war largely confined to southern Egypt. More than 1,000 people have been killed in the conflict.
Yasser el-Sirry, an Islamist sentenced to death in Egypt and living in exile in Britain, told Reuters he was taking the ceasefire seriously but could not yet confirm its authenticity.
"The initiative embarrasses the regime," Sirry said in a telephone interview. "The ball now is in the regime's court. It has to choose between stability or the continuation of violence."

Abdul Alim, speaking in military court at Heikstep army camp northeast of Cairo, said: "The Gama'a urges its brothers to stop military operations inside and outside Egypt and stop issuing all statements of incitement."

"This is a call from leaders of the Gama'a al-Islamiya at Tora prison," he added. He named them as Karam Mohamed Zuhdi, Nageh Ibrahim Abdullah, Abboud al-Zumur, Fouad el-Dualibi and Hamdi Abdul Rahman -- men imprisoned in connection with the assassination of President Anwar Sadat in 1981.
Zayyat told Reuters he hoped the government would reciprocate so that no uncontrolled members of the Gama'a al-Islamiya would break the ceasefire.
"I hope no security campaigns take place, otherwise elements inside the Gama'a may carry out operations as a reaction," he said. "Youngsters might come out and reject the appeal."
Abdul Alim, asked about the aim of the appeal on Saturday, told Reuters: "The unilateral truce is in the interest of Islam and Moslems. I am sure the leaders (at large) will observe it."
Another militant, Khaled Ibrahim, issued a similar appeal in February last year but other Islamists dismissed it as a personal gesture.
"It (the new appeal) is the fruit of one year of negotiations...The imprisoned leaders have been studying the best way (to do it)," Zayyat said.
The police say they have broken the back of the military wing of the Gama'a through raids on its hideouts and steps to prevent the organisation receiving help from abroad.

The number of Gama'a attacks has declined sharply since the mid-1990s, when the militants were killing about one policeman a day. In Cairo the organisation tried to kill the prime minister, the interior minister and the information minister.
In June 1995 a group of Gama'a ambushed President Hosni Mubarak's motorcade as he arrived for an African summit in the Ethiopian capital Addis Ababa. Mubarak escaped unscathed.
The group's aim is to overthrow the government and set up a strict Islamic state in Egypt.
